source_read: PMC full text PMC4158030 (published BMJ version) in the reader's own browser tab: abstract, all sections, Box 1, Table 1 (rendered as text), boxed key points, footnotes and reference list. Figure 1 (PRISMA flow diagram) is an image and was not needed for any number in the claim. Step 1 completed before the card was opened.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of this source. The claim is more cautious than the review's abstract, and its remark that the abstract's 'markedly attenuates or eliminates' is contradicted by the review's own Seattle 2012 summary is correct (Table 1; Results, 5th paragraph; Discussion, 7th paragraph). Two wording points: (1) 'more years with dependence' should be 'dependence at more of the follow-up interviews' (five interviews three years apart, 21 to 33, each asking about the past year); (2) the Young in Norway odds ratios of 1.5 and 1.6 were already adjusted for gender, not crude.
claims.note: Every number in the statement and magnitude that comes from this source was checked against Table 1 and the Results text and matches: n 522, 447, 808, 706, 1311; -3.465 and -13.828 (p<0.0001); OR 2.39 (1.10-5.20) and 5.75 (1.53-21.54), both against a first drink at 11 or older at a family gathering; -0.0631 (p>0.05); 0.3848 (p<0.0001); OR 1.68 (p<0.05, no interval); beta 0.44, then 0.53, 0.46, 0.45 and 0.46; OR 1.5 (1.2-1.9), 1.6 (1.3-2.1), and 1.2 (0.9-1.6) for both; search to 10 January 2013; five reports from four cohorts; no meta-analysis. One correction to the magnitude: 'no association with misuse or any dependence (ORs 0.96, 1.40 and 0.64 against a first drink at 11-14)' gives only the misuse odds ratios. The odds ratios for dependence at any follow-up were 1.49, 1.16 and 0.35 (all p>0.05; Table 1, Guttmannova 2011 row). Suggested: 'misuse ORs 0.96, 1.40 and 0.64, any dependence ORs 1.49, 1.16 and 0.35, all p>0.05, against 11-14'. Qualifiers the claim leaves out: the review warns that adjusting for peer variables may be overadjustment (Discussion, 3rd paragraph), which weakens attenuation as evidence of confounding; the Seattle 2011 sample was limited to people who started drinking before 21; the Rutgers sample was limited to people who completed every wave. The 'critically low' rating comes from the card, not from the source (confirmed in step 2).

anchors.extracted: Only five studies were eligible. Effects of age of first drink (AFD) on adult drinking and problems were supported, weakly, in some studies and not in others. The abstract generalizes that rigorous control for confounding markedly attenuates or eliminates any observed effects, which the review's own Seattle 2012 summary contradicts (see Table 1).

Eligibility: general-population cohort studies only; AFD = first drink of more than a few sips (studies of first intoxication or start of regular drinking only were excluded); at least 3 years between the initial adolescent AFD measurement and the alcohol outcomes; outcomes at age 18 or older (consumption, DSM/ICD dependence or problems, other harmful use); a reported magnitude of association; peer-reviewed only; no language or date limits; special populations such as children of alcoholics excluded.

Medline, Embase, PsycInfo and Social Policy and Practice searched from inception to 10 January 2013, plus backward and forward citation searching, 20 experts contacted and a related review's references screened. Abstracts screened by the first author only; full texts reviewed independently by both authors.
Narrative synthesis. Meta-analysis judged inappropriate because of heterogeneous methods and outcomes. Studies appraised for confounding, selection, attrition, recall and reporting bias.

Five studies, three published in the past 3 years. Four cohorts: three reports from two US cohorts and two reports from two Norwegian cohorts. Samples ranged from 447 to 1311. Cohorts were school-based or community-based.

anchors.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, Pedersen and Skrondal 1998 row
anchors.extracted: Oslo school cohort, n=522, follow-up 89%. AFD charted yearly (continuous); outcomes at 18-21. Structural equation coefficients: -3.465 for debut age on past-month consumption and -13.828 on the Rutgers Alcohol Problem Index, both p<0.0001. Roughly, a 10% delay goes with 35% less consumption. Confounders: only parents' and friends' norms and alcohol and tobacco use. The original authors acknowledged that stricter control would weaken the association.

anchors.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 1, Warner and White 2003 row
anchors.extracted: Rutgers community cohort (USA), n=447, follow-up 83%, restricted to people who provided data at every wave. AFD before 11 at a family gathering: OR 2.39 (95% CI 1.10-5.20). Before 11 elsewhere: OR 5.75 (1.53-21.54). Both are against AFD at 11 or older at a family gathering, for lifetime problem drinking by 30-31, adjusted for first-drink features, gender, SES and religion. In the fully adjusted multivariable model AFD was not significant (coefficient -0.0631, p>0.05). Feeling drunk at the first drink stayed significant (0.3848, p<0.0001).

anchors.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 1, Guttmannova et al 2011 row
anchors.extracted: Seattle Social Development Project, n=808 who started drinking before 21, follow-up 92%; outcomes every 3 years from 21 to 33. Misuse at any follow-up, vs AFD 11-14: <11 OR 0.96, 15-17 1.40, 18-20 0.64. Dependence at any follow-up: 1.49, 1.16, 0.35. All p>0.05. Chronicity of dependence (number of interviews with a past-year diagnosis): <11 OR 1.68 (p<0.05), 15-17 1.04. No confidence intervals given. Adjusted for gender, ethnicity, childhood poverty and adolescent tobacco, marijuana and other drug use. Starting regular drinking at 15-17 was consistently associated with misuse and dependence.

anchors.locator: Results, 5th paragraph; Table 1, Guttmannova et al 2012 row
anchors.extracted: Same cohort, subset n=706 (follow-up given as 100%). AFD <11 vs not and chronicity of dependence: bivariate beta=0.44 (p<0.05). Four models, each with demographic and family covariates: peer factors 0.53 (p<0.01), school 0.46, behavioural 0.45, substance misuse 0.46 (each p<0.05). The association was largely unaffected, and none of the three explanations tested (marker or confounding, developmental impairment, more adolescent substance use) was supported.

anchors.locator: Results, 6th paragraph; Table 1, Rossow and Kuntsche 2013 row
anchors.extracted: Young in Norway, national school cohort, n=1311, follow-up 82.4%. Exposure: binary, any drinking by 13-14 (from questions on the most recent drinking occasion). Single outcome wave at 26-27. Adjusted for gender only: frequent intoxication (10 or more times in 12 months) OR 1.5 (1.2-1.9); AUDIT 8 or more ('harmful alcohol use' in Table 1) OR 1.6 (1.3-2.1), both p<0.01. Adding adolescent conduct problems: 1.2 (0.9-1.6) for both, p>0.05.

Confounding was controlled most extensively by Warner and White, reasonably by Guttmannova et al and less by Rossow and Kuntsche. Overadjustment is possible, for example peer variables that may lie on the causal pathway.
Eligible studies may have been missed. Publication bias is judged a profound threat to any inference, and no birth-cohort study had reported on the question.
No included study came from a low- or middle-income country or from a country with a Mediterranean drinking culture. The consequences of early AFD may vary by culture.

Weak or absent associations after adjustment give some support to a marker hypothesis: an underlying vulnerability leads both to early drinking and to adult problems. The review notes, however, that the latest Seattle findings (Guttmannova 2012) rejected a marker hypothesis.

In the included studies (Warner and White; Guttmannova 2011), feeling drunk at the first drinking episode and starting regular drinking had larger associations with adult alcohol problems than AFD itself.

The authors conclude that it is not yet known whether starting to drink earlier leads to adult alcohol problems. The same paragraph lists the second Seattle report among the studies supporting 'the opposite possibility', which conflicts with the review's own summary of that report (Results, 5th paragraph; Table 1).

key_findings.correction: Optional addition: the any-dependence odds ratios, against 11-14, were 1.49, 1.16 and 0.35, all p>0.05 (Table 1). The claim's magnitude attaches the misuse odds ratios to 'misuse or any dependence'.

reporting_issues.note: Precision point: the printed criterion is 3 years between the initial adolescent AFD measurement and the outcomes (Methods, 2nd paragraph), so the late starters are a limitation of the design rather than a breach of the rule as written. The card's consequence says this correctly; its first sentence words the criterion a little more strictly than the source. The Seattle 2012 report also collected AFD up to 24, overlapping its outcome waves (Table 1).

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low: two critical items clearly not met (item 2, no protocol; item 7, no list of excluded studies). The overall rating does not depend on the strict reading of item 4. Items 5 and 6 (no single-reviewer abstract screening; no stated duplicate extraction) and item 9 partial yes (narrative appraisal, no tool) agree with my reading.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract's 'markedly attenuates or eliminates' and its policy recommendation go beyond four small cohorts, one of which showed an association unchanged by adjustment. The final paragraph also misclassifies that report.

missed: Rutgers odds ratios: both 2.39 and 5.75 are against a first drink at 11 or older at a family gathering (Table 1). The card and the claim give the place of the first drink but not the reference group.

Table 1 (Guttmannova 2011) also gives any-dependence ORs of 1.49, 1.16 and 0.35 and misuse-chronicity ORs of 1.20, 1.13 and 0.77, all p>0.05. The claim's magnitude should give the dependence ORs or stop attaching the misuse ORs to dependence.
